rules.name: One product log
rules.heading: Conventions / Where things live
rules.text: 1. **One product log** — Start every project, new or old, from one product log.

rules.name: Sprints and designs side by side
rules.heading: Conventions / Where things live
rules.text: 2. **Sprints and designs side by side** — Treat Sprints and designs as peers under the product log: a Sprint, the Developer's, delivers an Increment; a design, the Designer's, delivers a prototype and conclusions. Open a design when an item needs design, when Sprint refinement hits a hard point, or for a blank page (`conventions/product-log.md`, convention 2); it is not part of a Sprint. Whether a question needs a design sprint or the five modes is `../ideo-kernel/conventions/ideo-log.md`, convention 1. Decide item by item whether design is needed; a design's conclusions still land through a Sprint; an Increment need not be code — the Definition of Done says what it is. This departs from the Scrum Guide: see Departures.

rules.name: Three layers
rules.heading: Conventions / Where things live
rules.text:
3. **Three layers**

   | Layer | File | Commitment | Accountable | Facilitates |
   | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
   | 1 | Product log | Product Goal | Product Owner, with the Scrum Master | — |
   | 2 | Sprint log | Sprint Goal | Developer | Scrum Master |
   | 2 | Design log | Design goal | Designer | Scrum Master |
   | 3 | Increment: code or documents, as the Definition of Done says | Definition of Done | Developer | — |
   | 3 | Prototype: built to learn, never in an Increment; a design’s prototype stays with its design evidence | Design questions | Designer | — |

   The third layer is not a log and has no prescribed method; it relies on the skills of whoever does the work. Increments add up into the product. The design’s conclusions flow back; its working material, including the prototype, stays with the design and can be referenced by the Sprint that builds those conclusions (`../design-kernel/conventions/design-log.md`, convention 19). The standalone IDEO log has its own rule (`../ideo-kernel/conventions/ideo-log.md`, convention 4).

rules.name: Folders
rules.heading: Conventions / Where things live
rules.text: 4. **Folders** — `scrum/` holds all of the Scrum work: `ProductBacklog.md`; `ScrumBoard.html`, the board written from the logs, which keeps no state of its own (`conventions/board-log.md`); `sprint-NN-<suffix>/` with `SprintBacklog.md` and its working files; `design-<suffix>/`, unnumbered, with `DesignBacklog.md`, prototypes, and other working material; `ideo-<suffix>/`, unnumbered, with `IdeoBacklog.md`, prototypes, and working files; and `documents/` (convention 5). The active folders may still hold work that ended and is awaiting Review; read the log’s `Now` before resuming. This is the author’s layout; use your project’s own places if it has them.

rules.name: Where files go
rules.heading: Conventions / Where things live
rules.text: 5. **Where files go** — A file that serves only one log usually stays in its working folder and can be cleaned up when that work ends. The design’s original working material is the exception: retain it with the design, then move it with its log into the existing `scrum/documents/` archive at Review (`../design-kernel/conventions/design-log.md`, convention 19; `../sprint-kernel/conventions/sprint-log.md`, convention 17). Files serving the whole Scrum also go into `scrum/documents/`, and the logs reference them. A project can use its existing archive subfolders. The project’s own documentation, such as a user manual or API notes, stays where the project keeps it, such as `docs/` at the root.

rules.name: Working material
rules.heading: Conventions / Where things live
rules.text: 6. **Working material** — Keep working material out of the log itself; link to the retained design originals as convention 5 says. Key material of general use can go into the project’s memory or instructions, and a large important file goes into `scrum/documents/`. Retro lessons go only where `../sprint-kernel/conventions/sprint-log.md`, convention 18, says, never in instructions.

rules.name: Names
rules.heading: Conventions / Where things live

rules.name: Roles
rules.heading: Conventions / Who does what
rules.text:
8. **Roles** — On a Claude Code role command, invoke the kernels in the order shown before doing any role work.

   | Role | Home turf | Accountable for | Claude Code entry kernels, in order |
   | --- | --- | --- | --- |
   | Product Owner | The product log and its handoffs | Value direction; the Product Goal and Sprint Goals; which items enter a Sprint; the go-ahead; the items, decided with the Scrum Master; stage results and permissions to start or return (convention 12) | — (a person) |
   | Scrum Master | Sprint logs and design logs | Facilitating Planning and refinement; recording; tracking; reviewing the How and the Increment; serves the Product Owner; acts for them within a written handover, and the accountability stays with the Product Owner; decisions made under it are recorded | ideo → scrum → sprint → design |
   | Developer | The Sprint | The sprint log, the How, the Increment; the last check that nothing in refinement is unclear | ideo → scrum → sprint |
   | Designer | The design | Ideas, prototypes, and tests for a design, from Ideate on (the Product Owner and the Scrum Master settle its research and definition); conclusions back to the product log and the Sprint that asked | ideo → scrum → design |
   | Stakeholder | An outside view, or standing non-source chores | Looking as one row of the product log's stakeholder table; a PO assistant organizes logs, summarizes progress, relays settled work and maintains the board, but does not rank, decide, review or edit plugin files | ideo → scrum |

   In Claude Code, use the Skill tool one at a time, wait for success, and skip only calls already successful in this conversation. Stop and report a failed load rather than substituting a file read. In DSH, native role entries instead preload ideo and scrum in order, then load sprint and design as needed for the work. Subagents a role dispatches load the ideo-kernel and scrum-kernel skills too.

   The Product Owner, the Scrum Master, and the Developer keep the sprint log together; without a Developer, the Product Owner and the Scrum Master run the Sprint alone.

rules.name: Only the Product Owner must be human
rules.heading: Conventions / Who does what
rules.text: 9. **Only the Product Owner must be human** — The other roles may all be AI. This departs from the Scrum Guide Expansion Pack: see Departures.

rules.name: Ask the Product Owner
rules.heading: Conventions / Who does what
rules.text: 10. **Ask the Product Owner** — Whoever is unsure asks the Product Owner, unless the Product Owner has sent that kind of question elsewhere.

rules.name: Product Owner as Developer
rules.heading: Conventions / Who does what
rules.text: 11. **Product Owner as Developer** — When the Product Owner builds, they take part as a Developer, and the How is worked out with them.

rules.name: Product Owner decides between stages
rules.heading: Conventions / Who does what
rules.text: 12. **Product Owner decides between stages** — The Product Owner settles each stage’s result. Before starting or returning to a stage of a Sprint or a design sprint, wait for explicit permission for that stage and scope. Approving a result is not permission to move on, though one message can say both clearly. While waiting, record the result or why a return is needed, but do not start or delegate that stage’s work. A new session may resume the same stage within its recorded permission and scope; earlier permission does not carry over to a return. The Scrum Master acts for the Product Owner only within a written handover covering the particular decision; handing over a review or a choice inside a stage does not hand over a stage transition. Record who decided, the date and basis, and the stage and scope authorized, including the written handover if used. Keep the decision at the end of its stage chapter; if permission arrives later, add that dated decision without replacing the earlier one. Record first entry when opening the log. These are stage decisions, not reviews, formal acceptance, or approval of each step. Sprint decisions: `../sprint-kernel/conventions/sprint-log.md`, convention 24; design decisions: `../design-kernel/conventions/design-log.md`, convention 26.

rules.name: One Scrum Master per project
rules.heading: Conventions / Sessions
rules.text: 13. **One Scrum Master per project** — Each project has one session as its Scrum Master, leading its Developer, Designer, and Stakeholders. A session above several projects only summarizes; each project's facts stay in its own logs.

rules.name: Who gets which work
rules.heading: Conventions / Sessions
rules.text: 14. **Who gets which work** — Reviewing the work goes to the Scrum Master by default (`../sprint-kernel/conventions/sprint-log.md`, convention 14); when the Developer works in another session or tool, `../sprint-kernel/conventions/sprint-log.md`, convention 26, says how the two work together. Long-running upkeep — the board, summaries, tracking — goes to a standing Stakeholder session with a working identity the project writes down, such as PO assistant. That assistant relays only what the Product Owner or Scrum Master already decided; scope or item changes and go-aheads go through the Scrum Master, who chooses the receiving session. It does not rank, decide, review or edit plugin files; an independent outside view still comes from a fresh subagent. A small edit to one or two files the Scrum Master makes itself. Building goes to a new Developer session when a paragraph can brief it, or to a Developer that shares the Scrum Master's context when the work needs much of the discussion; such a Developer cannot review its own work.

rules.name: Working conventions
rules.heading: Conventions / About these conventions
rules.text: 15. **Working conventions** — Reference, not law. Each convention has a short name, for use in conversation, and only the exceptions carry a source label: a convention with no label is the author's practice — how the author works; **Supplement** — inferred by the author's assistant, not yet confirmed in practice; **Decide on the spot** — no fixed rule, decide when it comes up. When you override a convention, write what you did and why in the log's notes: the sprint log's Increment notes, or the chapter of the design log it concerns. The templates carry the flow; the convention files say how, and when a step may be skipped. They describe roles and steps, not the mechanics of any tool.

rules.name: Templates record outputs
rules.heading: Conventions / About these conventions
rules.text: 16. **Templates record outputs** — A template's chapters follow the flow, and its sections hold only what each step produced; how to do a step belongs in the conventions. A log made from a template keeps all of the template's headings, including the chapters filled in later, and adds no sections of its own; put work remarks in the sprint log’s Increment notes or the relevant design chapter. An optional explanation below a commitment table belongs in the commitment’s own section (convention 17).

rules.name: Goal fixed, plan flexible
rules.heading: Conventions / What stays fixed
rules.text:
17. **Goal fixed, plan flexible** — Each log has one fixed commitment: the Product Goal, the Sprint Goal, the design goal; the Definition of Done is not weakened either. Everything under a commitment — items, refinement points, acceptance criteria, the How, the chosen design solution — may change as you learn, and each log records what changed and why. Only the Product Owner changes a commitment, and only the Product Owner cancels a Sprint whose goal can no longer be met.
    Keep the product statement in the product log's section 1.1, the Product Goal in its section 1.2, the Sprint Goal in the sprint log's section 1.1, and the design goal in the design log's section 1.2. Each has one one-row table: the first cell is `Commitment` (`承诺` in a Chinese log), the second is the exact text, without bold. Keep one copy, not another at the file’s top; its section heading identifies it. The table is the only source of the current commitment. Optional reasons can follow below it; they are not part of the commitment or what a reader extracts from the table. Exact text on a stage decision line is a snapshot of the commitment at that time, not a second source; do not update it when the current goal changes. Give each goal one short name and keep using that name. An IDEO log has no commitment of its own: its For field points to the log it serves.
    The Scrum Guide says it this way. On the Product Goal: "They must fulfill (or abandon) one objective before taking on the next." During the Sprint: "No changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal", "Quality does not decrease", and "Scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned." And: "Only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel the Sprint."

blocks.text: > These are working conventions — the author's reading of Scrum and design thinking for solo + AI teams. They are less precise than the official guides. blocks.text: Each departure is stated here once, with its reason; the convention named in the last column points back to this table.
blocks.heading: Departures from the official guides

blocks.text:
| Here | The official guide | Why | See |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Only the Product Owner must be human | SGEP: the Product Owner and the Scrum Master "must be human", and "At least one Product Developer should be human" | One person works with AI and keeps the value decisions | Convention 9 |
| Designs sit beside Sprints | Scrum Guide: all the work "happen within Sprints" | A design delivers no Increment, may span several Sprints, and the Designer and the Developer are peers | Convention 2 |
| The Product Owner decides the items with the Scrum Master | Scrum Guide: "the Developers select items from the Product Backlog" | The Product Owner sets the value direction, and the others say how much fits | `conventions/product-log.md`, convention 12 |
| The How is a plan, and building waits for the go-ahead | Scrum Guide: how to build is "at the sole discretion of the Developers" | The Scrum Master and the Product Owner check the plan, because AI may drift | `../sprint-kernel/conventions/sprint-log.md`, conventions 7 and 8 |
| Checkpoints replace the Daily Scrum | Scrum Guide: the Daily Scrum is "a 15-minute event for the Developers" | AI works by session, not by day | `../sprint-kernel/conventions/sprint-log.md`, convention 10 |
| A reviewer is required | Scrum Guide: the Developers are accountable for "Instilling quality by adhering to a Definition of Done" | A Developer may drift, and a second look catches it | `../sprint-kernel/conventions/sprint-log.md`, convention 14 |
| No Sprint end date | Scrum Guide: Sprints are "fixed length events of one month or less" | AI works by session, so the Product Owner watches at checkpoints for a Sprint that drags on | `../sprint-kernel/conventions/sprint-log.md`, convention 2 |
blocks.heading: Departures from the official guides

rules.name: One product log
rules.heading: Starting
rules.text: 1. **One product log** — Write the product log from the template (`overview.md`, convention 1). For an old project, write it from what already exists — the README, the open issues, the old plans — and leave the history in version control; what cannot be written yet follows convention 2.

rules.name: Blank page
rules.heading: Starting
rules.text:
2. **Blank page** — Write into the product log what you can define; replace what you cannot with the matching item of a design, and let the design answer it. When the product and its Product Goal cannot be written, the IDEO methods alone will not make them clear; start from a design (design-kernel skill), which adds the design sprint, a prototype, and a test to those methods (the boundary between the design sprint and the five modes: `../ideo-kernel/conventions/ideo-log.md`, convention 1). The design's items stand in for the product log's like this:

    | The design log | Product log |
    | --- | --- |
    | The challenge | 1.1 Product |
    | The design goal | 1.2 Product Goal |
    | The design questions, once the test has answered them | 1.3 Definition of Done (the Outcome Done measures); the ones not answered become items |
    | The people at the top of the map | 2.1 Stakeholders |
    | The map | 2.2 Map |
    | The target (`../design-kernel/steps/2-3-pick-a-target.md`) | 3 Product Backlog Items, each placed on a step of the map |

    In a section a design is answering, say which design answers it and link to it; do not copy the design log. The stakeholder table can be written first, because a design uses role cards from its first stage.

rules.name: Facts first, then questions
rules.heading: Starting
rules.text: 3. **Facts first, then questions** — *Supplement.* Have the Scrum Master look up the facts itself; what the Product Owner must decide goes into one message, numbered, each question with a recommended answer.

rules.name: Product and Product Goal
rules.heading: Each part
rules.text: 4. **Product and Product Goal** — Keep the product statement in section 1.1 and the Product Goal in section 1.2, each in its own one-row commitment table as the template shows (`overview.md`, *Goal fixed, plan flexible*); the vision line is optional. The product log has no Now or Waiting for PO line: it has no stage; those lines belong to the Sprint, design, and IDEO logs.

rules.name: Two kinds of Done
rules.heading: Each part
rules.text: 5. **Two kinds of Done** — Outcome Done is evidence of value the product delivers to its stakeholders; Output Done is the quality standard for the whole Increment. The full Definition of Done stays in section 1.3. A Sprint chooses where to focus its checks, not which standards apply. Write standards precisely and keep only requirements that hold across the product, not ones that merely came up this time. Put item-specific or tentative requirements in the item’s acceptance criteria instead.

rules.name: Stakeholders in a short table
rules.heading: Each part
rules.text: 6. **Stakeholders in a short table** — List the stakeholders in section 2.1 in a short table, not a long profile per person. A Stakeholder subagent gets one row as its identity, and the AI fills in the details. If the table is empty, ask the Product Owner who belongs in it, and add the rows.

rules.name: Architecture as a map
rules.heading: Each part
rules.text: 7. **Architecture as a map** — Start section 2.2 with one map, drawn as `../design-kernel/steps/2-1-make-a-map.md` describes: actors on top, AI roles included, the ending at the bottom, five to fifteen steps between, as a Mermaid `flowchart TD`. Add a subsection only for a step that needs more words.

rules.name: No TBD
rules.heading: Each part
rules.text: 8. **No TBD** — Turn an unclear point into an item; a Sprint or a design works it out.

rules.name: Technical design stays out
rules.heading: Each part
rules.text: 9. **Technical design stays out** — Keep technical design out: modules and interfaces are the Developer's; they live in the Increment.

rules.name: Seven columns
rules.heading: Items
rules.text:
10. **Seven columns**

    | Column | What goes in it |
    | --- | --- |
    | # | PBI- and three digits, counting up: PBI-001, PBI-002, and so on |
    | Title | A short name |
    | User story | "As <someone from section 2.1>, I want …, so that …" |
    | Place | A step of the map, or a subsection of section 2.2 |
    | Status | Where the item stands: waiting, in Sprint NN, in a design |
    | Size | S — one or two sessions; M — three to five sessions; L — more than five sessions, to be split when refining |
    | Notes | Source, open points, draft acceptance criteria, refinement notes |

rules.name: Numbers, not ranks
rules.heading: Items
rules.text: 11. **Numbers, not ranks** — Number items to count them, and keep every number unique; ranking is another matter — moving an item up the list — and the Product Owner does it when an order is needed.

rules.name: Items with the Scrum Master
rules.heading: Items
rules.text: 12. **Items with the Scrum Master** — Let the Product Owner decide the items together with the Scrum Master, who serves the Product Owner; acts for them within a written handover, and the accountability stays with the Product Owner; decisions made under it are recorded. At Planning the Product Owner leads the selection, and the Scrum Master and the Developer say when it is too much or too little; the measure is the Sprint Goal, and the check when the rows are written is `../sprint-kernel/conventions/sprint-log.md`, convention 5. This departs from the Scrum Guide: see the Departures section of `overview.md`.

rules.name: Status lives here
rules.heading: Items
rules.text: 13. **Status lives here** — Write an item's status in the product log only; a sprint log names items by number.

rules.name: Refine any time, finish in the Sprint
rules.heading: Refinement
rules.text: 14. **Refine any time, finish in the Sprint** — Refine in the product log only to add detail; finish the refinement in the sprint log's section 2.2 (`../sprint-kernel/conventions/sprint-log.md`, convention 6). The product log has no refinement section.

rules.name: Seven steps
rules.heading: Refinement
rules.text: 15. **Seven steps** — Refine one item at a time in the seven steps of `../sprint-kernel/conventions/sprint-log.md`, convention 6. Acceptance criteria already written in full here are not repeated in the sprint log.

rules.name: Where refined content goes
rules.heading: Refinement
rules.text: 16. **Where refined content goes** — Put refined content where it belongs: a split-off item becomes a new row; long design content goes into the architecture, and the Place column points to it; short notes go into Notes; large material goes into `scrum/documents/` (`overview.md`, convention 5), referenced from Notes.

rules.name: Fresh at every Review
rules.heading: Keeping it fresh
rules.text: 17. **Fresh at every Review** — At every Review, move done items to section 3.2, one line each, with the source, usually the archived sprint log in `scrum/documents/`; delete outdated architecture text and resolved open points — what counts as outdated is `../sprint-kernel/conventions/sprint-log.md`, convention 17; send unfinished items back to section 3.1. Keep no revision record; version control keeps the history. Fresh means more than the items: the Review keeps the rest of `scrum/` fresh too (`../sprint-kernel/conventions/sprint-log.md`, convention 17).

rules.name: Goal fixed, plan flexible
rules.heading: Throughout
rules.text: 18. **Goal fixed, plan flexible** — Refine items and acceptance criteria at any time; let only the Product Owner change the Product Goal, and only on evidence against it. Write an item's change and its reason in its Notes, and a Product Goal change with its date and reason in section 1.2 (`overview.md`, convention 17).

blocks.text: > Working conventions: reference, not law — follow what fits, override what doesn't, note why. Source labels and short names are explained in convention 15 of `overview.md`, in the skill folder, beside `SKILL.md`. A convention with no label is the author's practice.

> Source: quotations from The Scrum Guide 2020 (Ken Schwaber & Jeff Sutherland), marked where they appear.

The product log is the first layer. Its template is `product-backlog-template.md`; the Scrum Master usually writes it with the Product Owner. Paths starting with `../` are relative to the scrum-kernel skill folder.

```mermaid flowchart TD A["Starting
conventions 1–3"] --> B["Each part
conventions 4–9"] A -- "the product cannot be written yet" --> D["A design answers it (design-kernel skill)"] D -- "conclusions flow back" --> B B --> C["Items
conventions 10–13"] C --> E["Refinement
conventions 14–16"] E --> C C -- "each Review" --> F["Keeping it fresh
convention 17"] F --> C ```
Convention 18 holds at every step; see Throughout, below.

rules.name: One board for the project
rules.heading: What the board is
rules.text: 1. **One board for the project** — Keep one page for the whole project: the product, the items not done, and every open Sprint and design. It answers one question without opening a log: where does the project stand, and what is each line of work doing. It is meant to be glanced at — hung on a screen, read from a few steps away, on a wide screen, a portrait screen, or a phone — so it shows few things, and shows them large.

rules.name: It owns nothing
rules.heading: What the board is
rules.text: 2. **It owns nothing** — The board only reads the logs. It keeps no state, and no log is ever changed from it. Delete it and write it again, and every fact is the same; only the time it was made differs. For that reason the page need not go into version control; the project decides, for example with a `.gitignore` entry.

rules.name: Where it lives, who writes it, and when
rules.heading: What the board is
rules.text: 3. **Where it lives, who writes it, and when** — Name it `scrum/ScrumBoard.html`, beside the product log. A cheap model writes it, because the work is copying and summarizing, not judging: a fresh subagent told to read this file and the template and to follow them, or a standing helper session of the Product Owner's. Write it when the Product Owner wants to look, or after a log has changed.

rules.name: The logs
rules.heading: What it reads
rules.text: 4. **The logs** — The product log is `scrum/ProductBacklog.md`. The open logs are `scrum/sprint-*/SprintBacklog.md`, `scrum/design-*/DesignBacklog.md`, and `scrum/ideo-*/IdeoBacklog.md`; nothing in `scrum/documents/`, which holds the archive. A Sprint or design that is open on another branch counts too: read its log as committed on that branch (git can show a file at a branch's latest commit), and give `branch <name> @ <commit>` as its source, the commit as its first seven characters. A log that is in this working copy is read from the working copy, with any change not yet committed, and its source is `working copy`. If one log is found on several branches, use the version with the newest commit.

rules.name: What it takes from a log
rules.heading: What it reads

rules.name: Maps
rules.heading: What it reads
rules.text: 6. **Maps** — The product log's map is the Mermaid diagram in section 2.2; a design log's map is the one in its section 2.1. A node's label is the text inside the quotation marks of `["…"]`, `("…")`, or `{"…"}`; arrows and their labels are not nodes.

rules.name: The overview
rules.heading: What the page shows
rules.text: 7. **The overview** — A tall flow diagram. At the top, a circle for the product. Below it, the items that are not done, in four groups: in a Sprint, in a design, up next, later; the later ones fade. Each item that sits in a Sprint or a design is joined by a line to that Sprint's or design's node on the right: blue to a Sprint, purple to a design, and a dashed line between a Sprint and the design made for one of its items. Pressing an item lights up where it goes. Pressing the circle, a Sprint, or a design opens its card. One colour, amber, is kept for "here": where the open work stands on the map.

rules.name: The cards
rules.heading: What the page shows
rules.text: 8. **The cards** — Each card has three layers. The product card: the Product and the Product Goal, word for word; the architecture as one line of a few stops, with "here" at the stop where the open Sprint is; the items not done, grouped. A Sprint card: the Sprint Goal, word for word; the route, its items in order with how many of their work items are done; the work items of chapter 3, done ones marked. A design card: only its own design goal (section 1.2), word for word; its own map as a short line of stops; an independent solution section. Show what was chosen and how it is used, even without a storyboard. When no solution is chosen, keep the section and say so. The foot of a card holds the Now line, folded away until opened, any IDEO log that serves it (convention 11), and where the log was read.

rules.name: What the page works out itself
rules.heading: What the page shows
rules.text: 9. **What the page works out itself** — These are never written in the data, so they cannot be wrong: a Sprint's name from its folder (`sprint-20-presentable` is Sprint 20); a short name from the text before the first colon of a goal, and from the text before the first `——` of an item's title; a design with no colon in its goal is named by its folder's suffix; the count of work items and how many are done; the order of the items; the links.

rules.name: Links and sources
rules.heading: What the page shows
rules.text: 10. **Links and sources** — The page is written to `scrum/ScrumBoard.html`, so a card links to its log relative to the `scrum/` folder (`sprint-01-alpha/SprintBacklog.md`), and only when its source is `working copy`. When the log is only on another branch, the card names the branch and the commit instead, so that no link is dead. Every card's foot starts with its folder's name.

rules.name: One block of data
rules.heading: The data
rules.text:
11. **One block of data** — The page draws itself from one JSON object in `<script type="application/json" id="board-data">`. These are its fields; those marked with a star are copied from a log, the others are summaries or plain values (convention 12):

    | Field | What it holds |
    | --- | --- |
    | `lang` | `zh` when the logs are written in Chinese, otherwise `en`; the labels on the page follow it |
    | `generated` | when the page was made, `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM` |
    | `product.name` | the words before the first colon of the Product commitment, or the whole commitment when it has none |
    | `product.statement`, `product.goal` ★ | the Product and the Product Goal commitments |
    | `product.source` | `working copy`, or `branch <name> @ <commit>` |
    | `product.map` | the architecture as a list of stops: `{"text", "note", "here", "branch"}`; `note`, `here`, and `branch` are optional |
    | `product.closed` | the number of rows in section 3.2 of the product log; the page calls them "done groups", because a row can be a Sprint, or a clean-up |
    | `items` | each item not done: `{"id", "title", "status", "size", "group"}`; the first four ★ |
    | `sprints` | each open Sprint: `{"id", "goal", "now", "items", "blocks", "source", "ideo"}`; `id` is the folder's name; `goal` and `now` ★; `items` lists the numbers in section 2.1; `blocks` is `[{"n", "title", "done"}]` for each row of chapter 3, `n` and `title` ★; `ideo` is optional |
    | `designs` | each open design: `{"id", "for", "goal", "now", "map", "solution", "story", "source", "ideo"}`; `goal` and `now` ★; `for` lists the item numbers the `From` field names; `map` is a list of stop texts; `solution` is `{"title", "text"}` or `null` when no solution has been chosen; `story` and `ideo` are optional |
    | `ideo` | nested in a Sprint or design: `[{"id", "now"}]`, `now` ★; include a still-open IDEO log exactly once, under the open Sprint or design log its `For` header field points to. A mention of `For:` inside the question is not the field; a folder name alone does not identify the host. |

rules.name: Copied, and summarized
rules.heading: The data
rules.text: 12. **Copied, and summarized** — What is marked ★ goes into the data exactly as the log has it: the same characters, the same language; never reworded, shortened, translated, or tidied. A long text such as a Now line is copied mechanically — with a command or a script — rather than retyped: a long text copied by hand loses a character. Only `product.map` and a design's `map`, `solution`, and `story` are summaries. A map stop's text is a few words cut from one node's label: leave out the step number (①, ②), anything in brackets (item numbers, file names), and the explanation after a colon; never reword. So `③ 写产品日志：Product · 架构 · PBI（product-log）` becomes `写产品日志`, and `⑥ 施工（sprint-log）` becomes `施工`. Keep the main line only — five to eight stops, none longer than about twenty characters — and leave out the people at the top, the ending, and every side branch except the design sprint, which is a stop of its own. The steps a Sprint goes through, one after another, are one stop, joined with ` → ` (`Planning → PO 放行 → 施工 → Test`). A design's `map` comes from its own section 2.1, in source order, without people, the ending, or side branches: five or six stops when the map has them, no invented stops; omit it when no map is recorded. On the product map, `note` holds the item numbers in the brackets of the stop's label, as `62 · 64`. `here` lists the ids of open Sprints and designs at that stop: a Sprint at the stop its Now line names (planning, building, or testing), a design at the design sprint stop; leave `here` out when no stop fits. `branch` is true for a stop beside the main line. A design's `solution` summarizes section 3.1: a short `title` for what was chosen and a short `text` for how it is used. Leave out a part the log does not give; a recorded choice without usage details is still a choice. Write `null` when no choice is recorded: drafts, sketches, or a storyboard alone are not a choice. Optional `story` is a short ordered list of `{"title", "text"}` frames from section 3.2 that illustrate the chosen solution; omit it without a storyboard. Add no facts to fill either field.

rules.name: Groups and order
rules.heading: The data
rules.text: 13. **Groups and order** — An item's `group` is `sprint` when its number is in an open Sprint's section 2.1; otherwise `design` when an open design's `From` field names it; otherwise `later` when its status says it is for later; otherwise `next`. Keep the items in the product log's order: the page puts the items of a Sprint or a design in that Sprint's or design's own order.

rules.name: Work items and items
rules.heading: The data
rules.text: 14. **Work items and items** — A work item belongs to an item when its Work item cell names the item's number as written, or the number alone, as `68-a`. A work item that names no item belongs to none. The page counts only these; when no work item of a Sprint names one of its items, that Sprint's route lists the items without a bar.

rules.name: Escaping
rules.heading: The data
rules.text: 15. **Escaping** — In the JSON, write every `<` as `\u003c`, so that no text can end the script early.

rules.name: Left out on purpose
rules.heading: The data
rules.text: 16. **Left out on purpose** — The page does not show what waits for the Product Owner, nor the five stages a Sprint passes through: the Product Owner asks the Scrum Master for those, and they change faster than a page is written. Items in the product log's section 3.2 are done or closed and are not shown, only counted. Leave out IDEO logs that serve only the product log, have no open host, or have concluded even if not yet archived. Read the state of the IDEO run itself from the `Now` line (for example, `本轮五模式已收尾` or `The IDEO run has concluded`, optionally after the mode); a next step such as `待收尾` or a mention of closed items is not a concluded run. A host whose own `Now` explicitly says the Sprint or design has ended is no longer open, even while its log awaits archiving; finishing one of its stages is not ending the host. This affects only nested IDEO entries, not the discovery of Sprint and design cards (convention 4). Do not add a card or a new log field.

rules.name: Steps
rules.heading: How to write it
rules.text:
17. **Steps** — Follow these steps:
    1. Read `scrum-board-template.html`; its first comment says how to use it.
    2. Find the logs (convention 4) and read what each one holds (conventions 5 and 6).
    3. Copy the template to `scrum/ScrumBoard.html` with a command (`cp`, `Copy-Item`), replacing the old page. Do not retype it.
    4. Write the data (conventions 11–16) and put it in place of the single placeholder line in the data block. Change nothing else on the page.
    5. Check the page (convention 18).

rules.name: Check
rules.heading: How to write it
rules.text: 18. **Check** — Check the page against the logs: the JSON reads; every ★ field is found in its log, character for character; every stop of a map is found in the log's map; every number in `items`, `for`, and `here` exists; open the page and see that it shows the board, not a message. Fix what is not.

rules.name: What the board does not do
rules.heading: How to write it
rules.text: 19. **What the board does not do** — Nothing on it changes anything: an item lights up where it goes, a node opens a card, and that is all. It edits no log and keeps no state between pages. Nothing becomes true because it is on the board.

The Scrum board is one page that shows where the project stands. Its template is `scrum-board-template.html`, beside this file; this file is also the brief for whoever writes the page. Paths starting with `../` are relative to the scrum-kernel skill folder.

```mermaid flowchart TD L["The logs
product log, open Sprint, design, and IDEO logs"] --> R["Read
conventions 4–6"] R --> D["Write the data
conventions 11–16"] D --> G["Put it in the template
convention 17"] G --> B["scrum/ScrumBoard.html
conventions 1–3, 7–10"] B -. "delete it, write it again" .-> L ```

rules.name: One branch, one folder
rules.heading: Opening
rules.text: 1. **One branch, one folder** — Give each Sprint one branch, with a separate working copy if wanted, and one folder, `scrum/sprint-NN-<suffix>/`: a two-digit number — the previous Sprint's plus one, starting at 01 — and a suffix saying what the Sprint is about. The folder's name is also the branch's name, and the tag's at close.

rules.name: No end date
rules.heading: Opening
rules.text: 2. **No end date** — Close a Sprint when its goal is met or the Product Owner stops it; the Product Owner watches at checkpoints for a Sprint that drags on. This departs from the Scrum Guide: see the Departures section of `../scrum-kernel/overview.md`.

rules.name: Small work, small Sprint
rules.heading: Opening
rules.text: 3. **Small work, small Sprint** — Open a Sprint even for work of half an hour to one session, each step shrunk to a line or two; the stage decisions and permissions, the review, and the close still happen (convention 24).

rules.name: Set the Sprint Goal
rules.heading: Stages / Why
rules.text: 4. **Set the Sprint Goal** — Set the Sprint Goal in the Product Owner’s own style. A project Sprint has one unifying value goal, even when it takes several items. A summary Sprint that serves as an index of different lines of work may list those lines within the same single-line commitment cell, not as separate commitments. The Product Owner leads, usually with the Scrum Master. In section 1.2, point to the full Definition of Done in the product log (§1.3) and name the checks to focus on this Sprint; leaving out a check here does not waive a standard. When even the Sprint Goal cannot be set, the ideo-kernel’s methods can help, as they can at any hard point (`../ideo-kernel/SKILL.md`). Share the goal and the checks with the Scrum Master and the Developer.

rules.name: Select the items
rules.heading: Stages / What
rules.text: 5. **Select the items** — Select the items and copy each into section 2.1 word for word, five columns — number, title, user story, place, size. As you write the rows, check the set against the Sprint Goal: every item serves it; add what it still needs, drop what does not serve it — never one just to fill the Sprint. Add a missing item to the product log first.

rules.name: Refine in seven steps
rules.heading: Stages / What
rules.text:
6. **Refine in seven steps** — Refine the items one at a time, led by the Scrum Master with the Product Owner; the Developer joins. Write into section 2.2 what was settled and who decided it, the acceptance criteria, and the tests. Take these seven steps:
    1. Take one item; it is the point of view.
    2. Confirm the point of view, copied from the goal or the item without change.
    3. Open the item into How Might We questions and unclear points.
    4. Place each point: the Product Owner decides it, the Developer proposes a solution, or it needs research — a question about what people want or what counts as good, with no ready answer — which the Product Owner settles by the boundary in the ideo-kernel's conventions (`../ideo-kernel/conventions/ideo-log.md`, convention 1): a design sprint, or the five modes.
    5. Cut the item into items of a few sessions at most, with acceptance criteria.
    6. Check that no questions are left — the Developer's about what is meant, the Product Owner's about what will be built: the Developer restates each point, and the Product Owner agrees.
    7. The Product Owner says when refinement is over.

rules.name: How is a plan, not steps
rules.heading: Stages / How
rules.text: 7. **How is a plan, not steps** — The Developer writes chapter 3 as a plan for making the selected items: the work items in order, each done within one session, each with its output and how to tell it is done; the key choices and their reasons; the known risks and open points. Write it to the level of approach, not steps: no step-by-step instructions, no file contents, no polishing of the plan; if you can write the steps, do the work. It is not the solution a design chose: if a design gave a solution, the plan is how to build it. The Scrum Guide's measure, "decomposing Product Backlog items into smaller work items of one day or less", becomes one session here. The Scrum Master and the Product Owner check the plan. This departs from the Scrum Guide: see the Departures section of `../scrum-kernel/overview.md`.

rules.name: Go-ahead
rules.heading: Stages / How
rules.text: 8. **Go-ahead** — Start building only after the Product Owner's go-ahead; approving a plan is not a go-ahead. Write it as the last line of chapter 3, with the date and how far it reaches: commit, merge, tag, release, push. The Product Owner may hand the review of the How, of new structures, and of full texts to the Scrum Master; write the handover in the log. The right to review the How is not the right to give the go-ahead (convention 24).

rules.name: Notes as you go
rules.heading: Stages / Increment
rules.text: 9. **Notes as you go** — Keep chapter 4, Increment notes, as the full record, so a new session can pick the Sprint up from the log alone. A session that picks up the Sprint goes by the notes and does not work everything out again. The notes take whatever form helps; they need not be a running account of what was done. The How in chapter 3 is a note too, and chapter 4 may refine it. When a work item is done, prefix its Done when cell in the chapter 3 table with `✓ <date>`, keeping the completion condition after it; an unmarked row is not done.

rules.name: Checkpoints, not stand-ups
rules.heading: Stages / Increment
rules.text: 10. **Checkpoints, not stand-ups** — Stop and check the work against the Sprint Goal at the end of each stage (convention 24), whenever the AI is stuck, and whenever the Product Owner asks how things stand. Stuck means one of these: waiting for a decision or a piece of information only the Product Owner can give, a block from outside the team, the same approach tried twice and failed, or the current How no longer showing how to reach the Sprint Goal; anything else is an adjustment inside the plan. This departs from the Scrum Guide's Daily Scrum: see the Departures section of `../scrum-kernel/overview.md`.

rules.name: Outline before full text
rules.heading: Stages / Increment
rules.text: 11. **Outline before full text** — Before writing a new lasting document or a new template, show its outline to whoever reviews it (convention 8): the headings at every level, each with one line on what its part will hold. Write the full text once the reviewer agrees; for a new template, the outline is its chapter list.

rules.name: Full text for review
rules.heading: Stages / Increment
rules.text: 12. **Full text for review** — Put a new lasting document's full text — word for word, not an outline — where the reviewer (convention 8) can annotate it, with the problems you found and a recommendation for each; change the source files only after approval. The version on disk wins: read before you overwrite.

rules.name: Tests: criteria first
rules.heading: Stages / Test
rules.text: 13. **Tests: criteria first** — In section 2.2, set the method and pass lines: what needs fresh evidence, what earlier evidence is expected to still hold, and which outcome signals must be shown in this Test. Commit the method and pass lines before running the Test; do not change them after seeing results. Check a script’s wrong calls one by one and write down why.

rules.name: A reviewer is required
rules.heading: Stages / Test
rules.text: 14. **A reviewer is required** — Have someone other than the builder review: the Scrum Master by default, or a Stakeholder or a fresh subagent when the Product Owner names one. A Stakeholder named as reviewer checks the work item by item against the Definition of Done and the acceptance criteria. When the Scrum Master also built the work, a fresh subagent reviews, checking only whether the work was done right. When the Developer only shares the Scrum Master's context, the Scrum Master still reviews: a shared context does not make it the builder. Brief a review subagent with the task, the project's rules, and the decisions already issued. The Scrum Master may send a subagent to do the review or to read a long diff, and still owns the conclusion. This departs from the Scrum Guide: see the Departures section of `../scrum-kernel/overview.md`.

rules.name: Product Owner acceptance when written
rules.heading: Stages / Test
rules.text: 15. **Product Owner acceptance when written** — Ask for formal acceptance only when the Definition of Done or the acceptance criteria call for it; sometimes a glance is enough.

rules.name: Record the tests
rules.heading: Stages / Test
rules.text: 16. **Record the tests** — In chapter 5, keep the Developer’s tests, the independent check, and any required Product Owner acceptance. Show the result of every Output Done standard and item acceptance criterion: link the new evidence or cite the old evidence and why it still holds. When a stated condition did not arise, record it and why it did not apply. An applicable standard without valid evidence does not pass, even if it was not a focus. Record the result of each Outcome Done signal separately from Output Done. An outcome required for this Test by the Sprint Goal, an item’s outcome or acceptance criteria, or another pass line set beforehand blocks a Test pass if unmet or unproven. Otherwise record a signal without evidence as not yet observed; report contrary evidence as not met and explain its effect. Do not claim the full DoD has passed on those signals. The Increment’s quality can pass on its own evidence; the Sprint Test passes only when all its required checks, review, and acceptance pass. Fix a problem within Test and test again; a return to an earlier stage needs a decision under convention 24.

rules.name: Review
rules.heading: Closing
rules.text: 17. **Review** — Close with a Review: compress the sprint log to its key decisions, rename it `sprint-NN-<suffix>.md`, and move it into `scrum/documents/` or the project’s existing archive subfolder there. An ended design is archived by the first Review that can read its complete log and all original material in its own checkout. Without that complete set, leave the design pending archival and do not move its log or material from another worktree. Archive its log as `design-<suffix>.md` and keep its original material together in a folder beside it, out of the active design path. Preserve the decision trail and verify that the archive is readable before updating references in this checkout. Hand off the old and new paths to any receiving Sprint working elsewhere; that Sprint first checks that the originals are readable at the new path in its own checkout, then updates its references there. While building, keep a readable old reference until the new one is available in that checkout. When the design is already archived on the target base (`main`), in this checkout, or in an integration branch ready alongside this Sprint, before the receiving Sprint closes check its actual material references — including those in its log being archived — and the originals against that combined target state, and update broken links before closing; an old link that works only in the current worktree is not sufficient. If the receiving Sprint closes while the design is still pending archival everywhere, keep the usable active reference, note the pending archival, and merge to `main`; the later archiving Review searches the whole project before its closing commit (convention 19 step 1) so those archived Sprint references are updated too, and reports any unmerged branches still holding stale active paths to the Scrum Master. Leave verbatim historical commitment snapshots unchanged. Report stale active paths on other branches to the Scrum Master, rather than changing those branches. Archive ended IDEO logs as `ideo-<suffix>.md`, using `../ideo-kernel/conventions/ideo-log.md`, convention 4, for their prototypes. Clean up ordinary working files in `scrum/`, including outdated ones in `scrum/documents/`; check that this does not remove design originals or break links to them, even when the receiving Sprint closes. Write the Stakeholders’ views and any changes to the product log or Product Goal into the product log and refresh it (`../scrum-kernel/conventions/product-log.md`, convention 17). For an outside view, the Product Owner or the Scrum Master — never the builder — summons Stakeholders from the product log’s table.

rules.name: Retrospective
rules.heading: Closing
rules.text:
18. **Retrospective** — Hold it as an action at close, with no chapter in the log. The Developer saves only the important, reusable lessons, one independently findable entry per lesson, in the project’s memory. Write enough to use each principle on its own: what broke or worked, why, and what to do next time. If the tool has no project memory, use the repository notes the project keeps for lessons, still one separately findable entry per lesson. Do not write a Sprint Retro summary, put lessons in `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md` or any other instructions file, or mix them with the plugin’s conventions. An index may point to the entries, not copy their text. If there is no important lesson, write no entry. Discard the rest: one-off session details, passing friction, and notes without a demonstrated reusable reason are not lessons; do not infer a cause to turn every remark into a principle. An especially good improvement goes into the Definition of Done with the Product Owner’s consent. Check whether the product log is still fresh.
    *Supplement:* ask where the Product Owner held up the AI — waiting for a decision, waiting for a go-ahead.

rules.name: One closing commit
rules.heading: Closing
rules.text:
19. **One closing commit** — Close in this order:
    1. Before the closing commit, search the whole project for old paths until none remain; the fixes go into that same commit.
    2. Make one closing commit with the changes Review and Retro actually made inside the repository. If project memory is outside it, or there is no important lesson, do not copy outside memory or create a Retro file to make the commit appear to contain both.
    3. Tag it with the Sprint folder's name; the tag's message says what the Sprint achieved.
    4. Merge into the main branch.
    5. Close the working copy.
    6. Delete the branch of the same name.

    Judge the project's health by `scrum/` alone: it holds all of the Scrum work (`../scrum-kernel/overview.md`, convention 4); elsewhere, usually only the README needs updating. Pushing and other outward actions need the Product Owner's consent.

rules.name: Goal fixed, plan flexible
rules.heading: Throughout
rules.text: 20. **Goal fixed, plan flexible** — Hold the Sprint Goal and the Definition of Done (`../scrum-kernel/overview.md`, convention 17). The How may change at any time; refinement points and acceptance criteria may be renegotiated with the Product Owner, or with the Scrum Master, who serves the Product Owner; acts for them within a written handover, and the accountability stays with the Product Owner; decisions made under it are recorded. Write each change and its reason in chapter 4, Increment notes.

rules.name: New work gets registered
rules.heading: Throughout
rules.text: 21. **New work gets registered** — New work goes into the product log as an item first; the Product Owner decides whether it enters this Sprint. The scope can be renegotiated; the Sprint Goal stays.

rules.name: The log is the handoff
rules.heading: Throughout
rules.text: 22. **The log is the handoff** — The header carries `> Now:` with the stage the Sprint is in and the last decision the Product Owner made, followed immediately by `> Waiting for PO:` with each pending decision's number and short question, separated by semicolons, or `None`. Update both with the log change that causes them; a session that picks up the Sprint reads them first, then checks the recorded permission for the stage and scope; the header is not itself permission to act (convention 24). Write no separate handoff documents: before a session ends or its context is shortened, write what matters into the log and update the header. At handoff or pause, commit within the authorized scope only if that commit is permitted; otherwise keep the uncommitted changes and record that status and where to resume. This handoff rule does not waive the required pre-Test freeze commit (convention 13) or the closing commit (convention 19): if commit permission is not recorded for those gates, ask for it before running the Test or closing. Stop at a complete point.

rules.name: Special cases
rules.heading: Throughout
rules.text:
23. **Special cases** — Two cases need a rule of their own:

    | Case | What happens |
    | --- | --- |
    | Something outside the team blocks the work | The Scrum Master tells the Product Owner at once |
    | A release is ready mid-Sprint | Release it with the Product Owner’s consent for outward actions (convention 19); the Sprint does not end |

rules.name: The Product Owner decides at the end of each stage
rules.heading: Throughout
rules.text: 24. **The Product Owner decides at the end of each stage** — Follow `../scrum-kernel/overview.md`, *Product Owner decides between stages*, at entry and on return. Record explicit permission to start Why when opening; if no Sprint Goal is set yet, do not record a placeholder as a commitment. The Product Owner sets the goal before What, ends refinement before How, authorizes building with the go-ahead (convention 8), authorizes Sprint Test separately from approving the Increment, and after Test decides to close or authorizes a return to the stage that needs work. A Developer’s checks while building are not Sprint Test. For the decision that sets the goal, put the exact text in the §1.1 table; before that decision is recorded and before each later stage decision, read the exact Sprint Goal from the table, and the Product Goal too if product direction is at issue. Check the work against what you read. If the required text cannot be read, stop at that gate. Keep the exact wording on the dated decision line as a record of the goal at the time, not a source for future decisions. Show the text to the Product Owner only when the goal has changed (including when Why sets it), when product direction is at issue, or when they ask.

rules.name: Ask the PO
rules.heading: Throughout
rules.text: 25. **Ask the PO** — Ask the Product Owner whenever you are unsure (`../scrum-kernel/overview.md`, convention 10), and in any case to: set the Sprint Goal (convention 4); select the items (`../scrum-kernel/conventions/product-log.md`, convention 12); say when refinement is over (convention 6); give the go-ahead (convention 8); decide at the end of each stage (convention 24); renegotiate the acceptance criteria (convention 20); decide whether new work enters the Sprint, and renegotiate the scope (convention 21); give formal acceptance, when it is written (convention 15); consent to outward actions such as a push (convention 19); and cancel a Sprint whose goal can no longer be met (`../scrum-kernel/overview.md`, convention 17).

rules.name: Developer in another session or tool
rules.heading: Throughout
rules.text: 26. **Developer in another session or tool** — The Developer may work in another session or another tool. When the two sessions can talk directly — another session in the same tool, or a Developer forked from the Scrum Master's session — they talk directly; a long review is written as a file and the message gives its path; the sprint log is still the record. When they cannot — the Developer is in another tool — the sprint log is the only channel: the two keep one working copy and take turns; whoever holds the turn commits within the authorized scope only if permitted — otherwise keeps the changes uncommitted (convention 22) — writes in the notes what was done, and says whose turn is next; what the reviewer finds goes to the Developer as a file the Product Owner passes on, and the Developer copies it into the log; the Product Owner carries only the word that it is the other side's turn. (These are examples, not rules.)

```mermaid flowchart TD A["Opening
conventions 1–3"] -- "PO authorizes Why" --> W["Why
convention 4"] W -- "PO sets the goal and authorizes What" --> H["What
conventions 5–6"] H -- "a hard point" --> D["Choose: a design sprint with its own gates, or IDEO methods"] D -. "what was learned" .-> H H -- "PO ends refinement and authorizes How" --> P["How
conventions 7, 8"] P -- "PO gives the go-ahead" --> I["Increment
conventions 9–12"] I -- "PO authorizes Sprint Test" --> T["Test
conventions 13–16"] T -- "fix on the spot, test again" --> T T -- "PO decides: close" --> C["Closing
conventions 17–19"] T -. "PO authorizes a return to building" .-> I ```
Conventions 20–26 hold at every step; see Throughout, below. Read each stage transition with convention 24; closing is a separate decision.

rules.name: Open a design for a question with no ready answer
rules.heading: Opening
rules.text: 1. **Open a design for a question with no ready answer** — When a question asks what people want or what counts as good, ask first whether a ready answer exists; if not, settle whether it needs a design sprint or the five modes (`../ideo-kernel/conventions/ideo-log.md`, convention 1); when it needs a design sprint, open a design and start with Empathize once the Product Owner authorizes it, not with solutions (convention 26). A blank page — the product and its Product Goal cannot be written yet — is a case of this: the design's conclusions fill the product log (`../scrum-kernel/conventions/product-log.md`, convention 2).

rules.name: Hard point, not the whole item
rules.heading: Opening
rules.text: 2. **Hard point, not the whole item** — From a Sprint, take out only the hard point that needs design; the rest of the Sprint goes on.

rules.name: Who
rules.heading: Opening
rules.text: 3. **Who** — The Designer is accountable for the design, and the Scrum Master facilitates and records; what the Product Owner decides is listed in convention 21. Empathize and Define — the challenge, the design goal, the design questions, the map, and the How Might We questions — are settled by the Product Owner with the session that plays the Scrum Master, who writes them into the log; the Designer takes over at Ideate. A design often needs only one session; whether that session also plays the Scrum Master, or a separate Scrum Master session runs, is the Product Owner's call. When one session plays both roles, write the same name in both fields of the header; it settles Empathize and Define with the Product Owner itself.

rules.name: Branch
rules.heading: Opening
rules.text: 4. **Branch** — A design opens its own branch when it opens; the on-the-spot decision is only its base — the Sprint branch or `main`. Do not name it `<sprint-branch>/<name>`: git cannot hold both `a` and `a/b` as branch names.

rules.name: Open a design
rules.heading: Opening
rules.text: 5. **Open a design** — Pick a suffix that says what the design is about, with no number; create `scrum/design-<suffix>/`; copy the template into it as `DesignBacklog.md`; fill in the header: where the design came from, the branch (convention 4), the Product Owner, the Designer, the Scrum Master, and the Now and Waiting for PO lines (convention 24). The folder holds the log, the prototypes, and the working material — sketches, gathered ideas, a grid of reactions; prototypes and working material never go into an Increment.

rules.name: Start from the people
rules.heading: Stages / Empathize
rules.text: 6. **Start from the people** — Start Empathize with the people concerned. When the Product Owner is the person concerned, ask first for concrete experiences — what happened, what they did, what they said — and only then ask for the Product Owner's call on what it means; otherwise start with users the Product Owner can bring. Documents and role cards come after. Write each finding where it belongs — in the challenge, the design goal, or the design questions — with its source, and say whether it is first-hand (what a person said or did) or second-hand (a record made for another purpose, or a role card's reading). Write the design goal as a vision: why we are doing this, and where we want to be — not how; a sentence that tells how belongs to Ideate. Keep the goal's one-row commitment table in section 1.2, as `../scrum-kernel/overview.md`, *Goal fixed, plan flexible*, says.

rules.name: Experts when needed
rules.heading: Stages / Empathize
rules.text: 7. **Experts when needed** — Once you have heard the people concerned (convention 6), write the challenge, the design goal, and the design questions; ask experts and do research only when these are still unclear. The experts are the Product Owner, in the conversation, and the role cards (`../scrum-kernel/overview.md`, convention 7), each played by a fresh subagent. Before asking experts, draft a rough map (`steps/2-1-make-a-map.md`); the log keeps what changed, not each interview. After asking the experts or doing research, refine the challenge, the design goal, the design questions, and above all the map once more: fill the gaps and redraw the map.

rules.name: Map and questions in the log
rules.heading: Stages / Define
rules.text: 8. **Map and questions in the log** — Draw the map as a Mermaid `flowchart TD`, actors at the top and the ending at the bottom, and keep it rough — five or six boxes and one loop. Draw the experience we want to reach, not what happens now: the way things are today, and where it hurts, go in chapter 1 with their sources (convention 6). *Departs from the book:* the book's step maps the situation as it is. Branches, exceptions, and solutions belong to the Ideate solution and storyboard, not in the map; if someone who never learned design cannot read it at a glance, a solution has been put inside. Write the How Might We questions against the map, with the challenge, the design goal, and the design questions of chapter 1 beside it. The map, together with the challenge, the design goal, and the design questions, is the point of view here; do not write a separate one. The Product Owner picks the How Might We questions that matter — no dot voting. There is no target step while the design runs; a design that began from a blank page picks its target when it ends (convention 19). If the map holds more than one design's worth of work, split the rest out into another design or into items (`steps/2-3-pick-a-target.md` shows how the book narrows a map).

rules.name: Lightning Demos (optional)
rules.heading: Stages / Ideate: diverge
rules.text: 9. **Lightning Demos (optional)** — When existing ideas would help, have subagents search for them in parallel; keep the list as working material, not part of the log. If subagents sketch (convention 11), the list is split among them, so that each starts from different ideas.

rules.name: Diverge before you converge
rules.heading: Stages / Ideate: diverge
rules.text: 10. **Diverge before you converge** — Whoever sketches a solution — a subagent (convention 11), or the main thread with the Product Owner (convention 12) — diverges first: use at least two methods, at least one of them from the ideo-kernel's Ideate methods, as `SKILL.md` requires (the first steps of the book's sketch, `steps/3-2-sketch.md` — notes, ideas, Crazy 8s — may be used alongside), go for quantity, and hold judgment back — and only then converge into a sketch. When you brief a subagent, tell it so. The ideas are working material; they do not go into the log.

rules.name: Isolated solutions (optional)
rules.heading: Stages / Ideate: converge
rules.text:
11. **Isolated solutions (optional)** — When several solutions that differ in approach are wanted, have several fresh subagents, unable to see one another, each sketch one complete solution in words or Mermaid. Give each its own materials — chapters 1 and 2 and its own part of the gathered ideas, or none until it has drawn — together with `steps/3-2-sketch.md` and the ideo-kernel Ideate methods, and give any summary apart too: one summary handed to all of them makes the sketches converge on one idea (in one design, two subagents given the same summary of reference examples both drew a subway map). Beyond chapters 1 and 2, give it nothing about how things are solved today — no current design, rules, or code — and tell it not to read the project's files. Each diverges first (convention 10). Some tools hand the project's instructions to every subagent anyway; when that happens, note it in the design log. Without subagents, the main thread and the Product Owner sketch together (convention 12).
    *Decide on the spot:* whether to use subagents at all, how many, and on which model, within how the Product Owner chose to run this round (convention 26).

rules.name: Talk with the Product Owner
rules.heading: Stages / Ideate: converge
rules.text: 12. **Talk with the Product Owner** — Whether or not subagents sketch, the main thread asks the Product Owner whether they have ideas and talks them over, diverging first (convention 10), without rushing to converge. If the Product Owner has no idea, the main thread sketches one direction on their behalf, as one of the lines. All the lines — the subagents' sketches if there are any, the Product Owner's ideas, the main thread's own — come back to the main thread, are merged, and only then does it converge (convention 13).

rules.name: Choosing is the key step
rules.heading: Stages / Ideate: converge
rules.text: 13. **Choosing is the key step** — Run the book's decision (`steps/3-3-decide.md`) in the conversation, led by the Scrum Master; have role-card Stakeholders give a straw poll if the Product Owner wants one. The Product Owner makes the final call, with no search for consensus. Put only the chosen solution into section 3.1.

rules.name: Combine or rumble
rules.heading: Stages / Ideate: converge
rules.text: 14. **Combine or rumble** — Combine winners that fit together; when two conflict, prototype both and let the test decide (`steps/3-4-rumble.md`). The Product Owner decides which.

rules.name: Storyboard
rules.heading: Stages / Ideate: converge
rules.text: 15. **Storyboard** — Write a storyboard of about fifteen steps in section 3.2 (`steps/3-5-storyboard.md`) only when the solution needs one before the prototype; the Designer writes it.

rules.name: Just enough prototype
rules.heading: Stages / Prototype
rules.text:
16. **Just enough prototype** — *Supplement.* Build in the design folder, following the chosen solution, real enough for honest reactions (`steps/4-1-fake-it.md`): made quickly for learning, not for production, while the surface the tester sees appears real. Keep it as design evidence under convention 19; keeping it does not make it an Increment. Subagents can build the parts while one session stitches them together; do a trial run against the solution and the design questions before testing, and write what it found in chapter 5. List each part of the prototype in chapter 4 with the design question it tests.
    *Decide on the spot:* how real the prototype must be when the product has no screen — a document, a service, a process; agree it with the Product Owner.

rules.name: Role-card test
rules.heading: Stages / Test
rules.text: 17. **Role-card test** — Test with role cards, each a fresh subagent given only its card, the prototype, and the tasks; the Product Owner tests too. The Designer runs the Five-Act Interview (`steps/5-2-interview.md`); a grid of reactions is working material; chapter 5 keeps who tested, what showed up, and the answer to each design question. The book tests five customers; here, test with the role cards the prototype is about — those who would meet it — and leave out the rest, and add runs while the patterns are unclear. When the thing is for the Product Owner alone, the Product Owner testing it is enough: do not make up a role card.

rules.name: Write the criteria before the test
rules.heading: Stages / Test
rules.text: 18. **Write the criteria before the test** — Before testing, write down in chapter 5 what would count as a yes, a no, or a not yet for each design question, and what role cards cannot show: they are subagents reading a card, not real people.

rules.name: When the design ends
rules.heading: Ending
rules.text: 19. **When the design ends** — End the design when the Product Owner decides its questions are answered, or stops it (conventions 21 and 26). Write the conclusions into the product log as `../scrum-kernel/conventions/product-log.md`, convention 2, says, and pass them to the Sprint that asked; for a blank page, pick the target (`steps/2-3-pick-a-target.md`), split it into items, and let the Product Owner order them. Mark the design concluded and awaiting archival in its existing `Now` line. Keep the log and all original design working material together until archival: prototypes, sketches and rejected options, demos, reviews, synthesis, and other material used in the design. From the relevant chapter, link to the originals or the folder that holds them; a summary or a commit ID alone is not enough. If a Sprint builds the conclusions, link from that Sprint to the prototype as a specification; do not leave its only copy in a Sprint working folder. Keep the material whether or not a Sprint will build the conclusions. It is design evidence, never an Increment. When the Product Owner explicitly permits the commit, merge, and branch cleanup, handle the branch as `../sprint-kernel/conventions/sprint-log.md`, convention 19, says: merge into its base (convention 4), then delete it; pushing and other outward actions require the Product Owner's explicit consent. A design has no Review or Retro of its own. After it ends, the first Sprint Review that can read its complete log and all original material in its own checkout archives them (sprint-log convention 17). A Review without that complete set leaves the design pending archival; it does not move material from another worktree. Hand off changed paths to any receiving Sprint, which updates its references only once it can read the originals at the new path in its own checkout. A usable old reference may remain while building, not as the closing check: when the design is already archived on the target base (`main`), in this checkout, or in an integration branch ready alongside it, before that receiving Sprint closes check its actual material references — including those in its log being archived — and the originals against that combined target state, rather than trusting an old link just because it still works in the current worktree; update broken links before closing. If the receiving Sprint closes while the design is still pending archival everywhere, keep the usable active reference, note the pending archival, and merge to `main`; the later archiving Review searches the whole project before its closing commit (sprint-log convention 19 step 1) so those archived Sprint references are updated too, and reports any unmerged branches still holding stale active paths to the Scrum Master. Do not close with broken material links or rewrite verbatim historical commitment snapshots. Next to the ending decision, leave a line or two on what the design taught about how to work, as input to the Retrospective of the Sprint that archives it, not as the Retro record itself.

rules.name: IDEO in every stage
rules.heading: Throughout
rules.text: 20. **IDEO in every stage** — Each stage of the design sprint stands on one IDEO mode: take the methodology from the mode the stage maps to, as `SKILL.md` requires. (The five modes are not the design sprint: `../ideo-kernel/conventions/ideo-log.md`, convention 2.)

rules.name: Ask the PO
rules.heading: Throughout
rules.text: 21. **Ask the PO** — Ask the Product Owner whenever you are unsure (`../scrum-kernel/overview.md`, convention 10), and to settle each stage result and authorize entry or return, including how this round of Ideate will diverge (convention 26); set or change the design goal (convention 25); pick the How Might We questions that matter (convention 8); choose the solution and decide between combining and a rumble (conventions 13–14); agree how real the prototype must be (convention 16); decide that the design ends (convention 19); and explicitly permit git actions (commit, merge, branch deletion, push) before they run (conventions 19, 24, and 26).

rules.name: Five chapters, not five days
rules.heading: Throughout
rules.text: 22. **Five chapters, not five days** — Write one chapter per stage — Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test — not the book's Monday to Friday, and no notes section. Each chapter records what its stage produced, not the steps taken.

rules.name: Renamed terms
rules.heading: Throughout
rules.text: 23. **Renamed terms** — See the first paragraph of `SKILL.md`.

rules.name: Resume from the header
rules.heading: Throughout
rules.text: 24. **Resume from the header** — Keep `> Now:` in the header with the stage and next step, followed immediately by `> Waiting for PO:` with each pending decision's number and short question, separated by semicolons, or `None`. Update both with the log change that causes them; a session that picks up the design reads them first, then checks the recorded permission for its stage and scope (convention 26) and any recorded git permission (convention 21). Neither `Now` nor permission to enter or resume a stage authorizes committing, merging, or pushing by itself. Before a session ends or its context is shortened, write the half-finished work into the chapter it belongs to and update the header. Commit within the authorized scope only if the Product Owner explicitly recorded commit permission for it; otherwise keep the uncommitted changes and record that status and where to resume.

rules.name: Goal fixed, plan flexible
rules.heading: Throughout
rules.text: 25. **Goal fixed, plan flexible** — Sharpen the design goal during Empathize; once it is set, only the Product Owner changes it. The questions, the map, and the solution may change with what the work shows; write what changed and why in the chapter it belongs to (`../scrum-kernel/overview.md`, convention 17).

rules.name: Gates between stages
rules.heading: Throughout
rules.text:
26. **Gates between stages** — Wait for explicit permission to enter or return as `../scrum-kernel/overview.md`, *Product Owner decides between stages*, says. Record permission to start Empathize when opening; if there is no design goal yet, do not record a placeholder as a commitment. Stage entry or return permission covers only that stage's design work and does not by itself authorize a commit, merge, or push; if git actions are permitted, record how far that permission reaches (for example, commit on the design branch; merge at ending decided separately; no push) on the stage or ending decision line. Before starting Ideate, the Product Owner settles how this round will diverge. Until that and entry are clear, do not gather ideas for the round, diverge, sketch, or delegate those tasks. Record the arrangement in chapter 3 before the solution section. Choosing a solution is not permission for Prototype, and a trial run is not permission for design Test. When the stage first sets a design goal, put its exact text in the §1.2 table. Before recording that decision and before each later stage decision, read the exact design goal from the table — and the Product Goal when product direction is at issue — then check the work against it and the table below. If the required text cannot be read, stop at that gate. Keep the exact wording on the dated decision line as a record of the goal at the time. Show the text to the Product Owner only when the goal has changed, when product direction is at issue, or when they ask. When a stage shows an earlier answer was wrong, report it and wait for permission to return; after Test the Product Owner decides whether to end the design or authorizes the return.

    | Stage | The log holds | The check |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | Empathize | the challenge, the design goal, and the design questions, with the source of each finding | The findings come from the people concerned — what they did, what they said, where the two differ — not from a pile of facts |
    | Define | the map and the How Might We questions the Product Owner picked | The How Might We questions were written against the map and the challenge, the goal, and the questions of chapter 1 |
    | Ideate | the chosen solution, and the storyboard if one was written | Whoever sketched diverged before converging, and when several sketches were drawn, they differ in approach, not only in detail |
    | Prototype | the parts of the prototype, each with the design question it tests | It is rough and quick: built to learn, not to deliver |
    | Test | the criteria written beforehand, what the trial run found, who tested and what showed up, and an answer to each design question with where it flows back | The answers come from real reactions, and "we were wrong" counts as an answer |

    At each gate ask: would someone who never learned design have produced the same thing? If so, the stage missed its focus.

rules.name: A small design is still a design
rules.heading: Throughout
rules.text: 27. **A small design is still a design** — Whether a question opens a design at all is settled by `../ideo-kernel/conventions/ideo-log.md`, convention 1. When the Product Owner opens a design that is small — about one session of work — still keep the log, shrink each stage to a line or two, and still keep the stage decisions and permissions under convention 26. Skip no stage, least of all Empathize and divergence (convention 10).
